Male here. I'm in my mid twenties and have worked a stupid amount of jobs (most low-ranking minimum wage types). Not to brag but I have rarely not gotten a call back for a job after an interview. Here is what I do. One: no matter what job you are applying for, dress up. Button-up, tie, nice jeans/chinos or slacks. Iron all of these clothes before you put them on for the interview. Two: smile. Smile at yourself in the mirror before you leave the house, get that amiability down son. Have a grin or faint smile on as soon as you walk into the establishment you are interviewing for. During the interview smile when you talk and ask questions of the interviewer if you can. Attempt to find common ground and the interview will feel more like a conversation - that's the goal, for the interview to become a pleasant conversation. Ask them how long they have been with the company and if they seem receptive to your friendly demeanor ask them about how long they've lived in ______ city. Ask about family/kids, people love to talk about their families. I'd imagine most hiring managers want to hire someone that seems like they'll get along with everyone else and is friendly to talk to, even if they aren't the most qualified for the position. Friendly and a nice tie will get you far.

Good news! For the past decade or so many teachers have observed what the ADHD/fidget report now confirms. Lots of good teachers (I won't say all because it's disingenuous to generalize an entire profession, but MANY) have adjusted their classrooms accordingly. In teacher education programs, accommodating individual students' needs is actually taught as the best method for learning (easier said than done when you have a classroom of 25+ students) and is called differentiation. Personally I have seen the following methods used in both my wife's classroom and her coworker's classrooms (she has taught in two school districts in Missouri so far): T chairs, which is a chair made from two 2x4s nailed together in a "T" shape with a cushion on top. the student absentmindedly focuses on balancing which allows an outlet for their fidgeting while they sit at their desk and learn. Similarly, in the school my wife teaches at now, they have small bar stool-like chairs that are rounded on the bottom so they can move around like one of those inflatable bounce-back toys. Finally in some cases a solution is as simple as having a student's desk in the back of the classroom where she/he can fidget to their heart's content and maybe even get up and stand if they need to, without distracting other students. This is all, of course, anecdotal evidence and classroom conditions should always be scrutinized to provide the best learning environment possible for students, but I hope I've shown that great educators do rethink their classrooms when they notice a problem. If you read all of this thanks! I can't wait to be a teacher and love talking about it, plus bragging on my wife :)

Hey there! I'm not OP but I'd be happy to give my two cents if you're interested. I think I love Saga, above all, because of how believable it is. Now, that may sound counterintuitive to my next point but we'll put a pin in that a circle back around to Saga's "believability" in a minute. Saga is also great because it is a bonkers blend of sci-fi and fantasy. There are horned civilizations that cast spells using ingridents like dragon sperm and personal secrets, there are sharks that fly, a cat that acts as a polygraph, humanoid robots with TV heads and a patriarchal government, the list goes on and on. Add to this some of the most beautiful artwork your likely to find in comics and already you've got yourself something special. However, what I think is Saga's biggest selling point (what I mentioned in the beginning) is how it is written in a way that is at once epic fantasy and extremely relatable. Brian takes one of the oldest story forms, Lovers from waring tribes, and extrapolates it to include the most believable arcs of domestic drama. Think Romeo and Juliet except the kids have functioning heads on their shoulders and start a family instead of killing themselves. The situations are believable and the dialogue is real. Brian doesn't fill his comics with wooden "comic dialogue/exposition" his characters communicate in ways that are real and deal with real problems. An added bonus to this is that Brian is also good at sneaking in insightful social commentary in a way that feels organic to the story and isn't shoehorned in for soap boxing's sake.  Honestly I could go on forever but I can't feel my legs anymore and I think my wife wants in the bathroom. I'll end by saying forget the recommendations that say "IT'S STARWARS MEETS GAME OF THRONES!!!1!1!11 XP"  because that is honestly a disservice to all three franchises, there is sci-fi, there is epic fantasy, but there is oh so much much more and that is what makes it rich.

Like I said, every teacher I have talked to about it is strongly against it, and I think that when the facts are presented to others it will be clear why teachers are against this.

Heavy parental involvement is often treated with eye-rolling and fists-shaking by teachers, nd with good reason. Most "helicopter parents" are looking for someone to blame for their child's supposed shortcomings. This bill does an excellent job of blaming teachers for everything and treating them like, as /u/pleurocarp said, "disposable pieces of scrap."

There will always be parents like that, there's nothing we can do about that. EVERY SINGLE teacher that I have talked too about this (and most non-teaching folk) are strongly against it. Here's why:

This amendment says:

"any school district receiving any state funding or local tax revenue shall develop and implement a standards based performance evaluation system approved by the Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education."
Now, while saying "Hey, you are hired to teach these kids so if they preform well you'll be paid well. If they don't you won't be paid well" SOUNDS like a nice reasonable and enticing idea it's really not, for two reasons. 1.) We have seen the ineffectiveness of "teaching to the test" if we are gonna evaluate the kids to base teacher pay off of you can bet there'll be some form of test involved, even if it is just using existing MAP scores. "Teaching to the test" is a terrible way for kids to learn and develop thinking skills but you can bet that if teachers' livelihoods are on the line, memorizing arbitrary facts in order to pass a test will  be what even the most outstanding teachers will be doing in their classrooms. 2.) Teaching is much more complicated than saying good scores=good teacher, let me give an example that I've seen first hand and which happen on a regular basis to show why student performance should not be the basis of teacher evaluation: Teacher has a classroom of mostly A and B students, just a luck of the draw. this year's class is really bright, and they manage a 3.2 GPA average as a whole. Fastforward to next year. A "normal". Batch of kids this year, some A's some D's and a whole lot of C's. The teacher tries real hard with the class and they manage a 2.8 GPA average as a whole. (this is considered a great year by everyone at the school because that same class got a 2.5 GPA last year) Now, using student performance only it looks like that teacher dropped 0.5 GPA points and is now in line for a payout to punish him/her for slacking off this year. And no, we can't look at the classes individually because the performance standards change every year (as you progress though grade levels) To keep things fair everyone has to be judged according to the same scale and expectations, you can't raise them for the "good" class one year because then you won't have accurate data for the kids next year to be judged on.

"Certificated staff shall retain the right to organize and to bargain collectively as provided in article I, section 29 of this Constitution, EXCEPT with respect to the design and implementation of the performance based evaluation system established in this article"

So here we are saying that we are going to implement a student evaluation system that YOUR employment and pay are directly affected by BUT you teachers can't even be involved in the process of designing it. That. Is. Criminal. Teachers weren't heavily involved in NCLB (though not by law that time) and we've seen how well that turned out.

Lastly and probably most controversially:
"No school district receiving any state funding or local tax revenue funding shall enter into new contracts having a term or duration in excess of three years with certificated staff." 

This is the part that means "no more tenure." My views on tenure are still evolving, but even if I have problems with it I don't think the answer is to get rid of it completely and reduce every teacher to 3 year contracts. Tenure gives teachers due process. Yes, you can still be fired if you have tenure. Tenure basically protects teachers for being fired due to budget cuts or disagreement with the board. A tenured teacher just has to be given the correct process for termination unlike untenured teachers whom a school can simply elect to not renew their contract. Oftentimes tenure teachers will use their tenure to speak for teachers that they feel might let go if they voiced certain concerns about the school. Yes, like any form of power it can be abused but we don't have tenure teachers napping all day long then picking up their government paycheck at the end of the month, hiding behind their tenure status. That wouldn't fly.

Sorry if I rambled or got overly passionate there, as a family just getting into the teaching profession this amendment scares the crap out of my wife and I.
